Perspective

Both sides of the
same workforce.

I arrived in Canada and built this career from the ground up, taking classes between long shifts. I started on the frontline. I manage HR now. Nothing about that order was accidental, and it is still the most useful thing I bring to the work.

Jan 2019 to Jun 2022 · On the floor

What the policy felt like

I worked the shifts, covered the gaps, and watched capable officers leave over things that had almost nothing to do with pay. A schedule changed without notice. A complaint that went nowhere. A promotion no one could explain. From that side of the workforce, an HR process is not a document. It is something that happens to you.

Jun 2022 to present · In the office

What the policy has to do

I now own those processes: how a vacancy gets filled, how a complaint gets investigated, how a decision gets documented and explained back to the person it affects. I write them knowing how they read at the other end of the shift, which is why I care as much about whether a manager can actually follow a process as whether it is technically correct.

People do not leave because of policies.
They leave because of experiences.

Having worked on both sides, I have seen what builds trust, what breaks it, and why good employees choose to stay or go. That is the lens I bring to recruitment, employee relations, and every investigation I run.

Case studies

How I approach
real HR problems.

Each case reflects a real situation I handled. Details have been generalized so that no individual, client, or site is identifiable.

Bringing an 80-requisition backlog under control

The story

When active requisitions climbed to around 80, the issue was bigger than simply finding more candidates. I needed to give recruitment, scheduling, and operations one clear view of what was urgent, what was already in progress, and where candidates could realistically be placed.

Challenge

Too many requisitions were moving at the same time, priorities changed quickly, and the team needed a more organized way to follow every vacancy.

What I did

I introduced a live tracker, grouped similar vacancies, used group interviews where appropriate, contacted agencies directly, and held regular placement discussions with operations. I also trained a new recruiter in three days so the team could contribute quickly.

Result

The active backlog dropped from approximately 80 requisitions to 17, while I continued supporting 300 to 400 hires per year.

Hiring 100 people in two weeks

The story

A major sporting event created urgent staffing pressure across our existing condominium, commercial, residential, retail, and mobile sites. Although the guards were not working directly at the event venues, the increased demand affected the entire operation.

Challenge

We needed a large number of licensed and suitable guards within two weeks, without lowering screening standards or creating confusion during onboarding.

What I did

I organized targeted sourcing, walk-in and group interviews, licence and experience checks, shared tracking sheets, and daily coordination with operations. I kept candidates moving through each stage and made sure the placement conversation happened before the final offer.

Result

We vetted and deployed 100 people in two weeks, and the related surge-hiring project was completed on time and under budget.

Reducing overtime through better staffing

The story

Overtime was not only a payroll number. It showed where vacancies, onboarding delays, and placement decisions were putting pressure on the operation. I treated it as a workforce-planning issue rather than a stand-alone HR metric.

Challenge

Open positions and slow placement decisions were creating repeated coverage gaps across client sites.

What I did

I connected recruitment priorities to site-level overtime, aligned candidate pipelines with upcoming vacancies, followed onboarding timelines closely, and worked with scheduling and operations on faster placements.

Result

Overtime fell from 3.68% to 0.35%.

Building a visible growth pathway

The story

Employees often asked what they needed to do to move beyond a guard position. There were training opportunities, but the steps, eligibility rules, and connection to performance were not always easy to understand.

Challenge

The business needed a structured development pathway that employees could follow and managers could apply consistently.

What I did

I designed the Squire → Ambassador → Specialist pathway: the policy, the eligibility and enrolment process, the employee and manager communications, and the link to training and performance reviews. Compensation bands were set by management.

Result

Employees gained a visible progression path, and the framework supported retention planning and union discussions.

Also handled

Six further cases, in brief.

Launching a new site in four days
The story

A new client location needed 40 guards almost immediately. The timeline left very little room for delays, and every hiring decision had to consider availability, commute, experience, and the actual shift pattern.

Challenge

The site needed to open on schedule, but fast hiring would not help if candidates later declined the location or could not maintain the required availability.

What I did

I worked backwards from the launch date, matched interview questions to site conditions, confirmed commute and schedule expectations early, and coordinated onboarding, uniforms, and placement with the operational team.

Result

Forty guards were hired in four days, allowing the site launch to proceed on schedule.

Redesigning the pre-hire assessment
The story

Candidates were sometimes being hired before they fully understood our policies and expectations. When training happened after hiring, some people withdrew late in the process or were not the right fit for the client.

Challenge

The process created avoidable post-hire attrition and used training time on candidates who had not yet demonstrated the required judgment or written communication skills.

What I did

I moved the learning and evaluation stage ahead of the employment offer. The five-hour Placement Assessment included 3.5 hours of policy and procedure training, followed by a 1.5-hour quiz and written report, with a 70% passing requirement.

Result

The assessment gave us a more consistent way to evaluate judgment, policy understanding, communication, and client fit before placement.

Standardizing discipline in Dayforce
The story

Different managers documented corrective action in different ways. That made letters slower to prepare and increased the risk of missing important facts, previous warnings, or the correct policy reference.

Challenge

The company needed a consistent process that still allowed each case to reflect its own facts and level of seriousness.

What I did

I created standardized reprimand and disciplinary letter templates in Dayforce, organized the required sections, and built the workflow so completed documents were saved to the employee record.

Result

Managers received clearer guidance, letters became faster to prepare, and employee files were more consistent and easier to review.

Using investigation findings to guide fair decisions
The story

I regularly support managers with attendance, misconduct, conflict, and policy concerns. In many cases, the first request is for immediate termination, but the available evidence does not always support that response.

Challenge

The organization needed decisions that were timely and operationally practical while still being fair, documented, and appropriate in a unionized environment.

What I did

I handled intake, evidence review, interviews, credibility assessment, and written findings. I then coached managers on whether the facts supported coaching, a warning, progressive discipline, further investigation, or another outcome.

Result

I became the primary HR contact for employee relations, supporting 11 to 12 managers and handling roughly 6 to 7 matters in a typical week, ranging from short fact-finds through to formal investigations.

Handling an accommodation case without making it disciplinary
The story

After a workplace incident was reported, the immediate question was whether it was safe for the employee to continue working and commuting. The situation needed a health and safety response, not assumptions about attendance or commitment.

Challenge

We needed reliable information about functional abilities before deciding on work, restrictions, or placement, while keeping the communication respectful and neutral.

What I did

I explained the temporary removal as a precaution, requested a Functional Abilities Form, reviewed the stated restrictions, and kept the employee informed about next steps and the return-to-work review.

Result

The case remained focused on functional abilities and safe placement, with a clear record showing that the action was precautionary rather than disciplinary.

Explaining a union-sensitive payroll question
The story

An employee questioned how overtime, statutory holiday hours, and training time had been calculated in Dayforce. The concern could not be answered with a general payroll explanation, because the collective agreement and the no-pyramiding rule both mattered.

Challenge

The employee needed a clear answer, while the company needed to apply the same CBA and overtime rules consistently.

What I did

I separated each category of hours, reviewed the overtime threshold and statutory holiday treatment, confirmed how the provisions worked together, and explained the calculation in plain language.

Result

The employee received a transparent breakdown, and the response protected consistent application of the collective agreement.
